t65t_sp5p2d5: Telling it like a story doesn't make it made up, and it doesn't prove you remember it right. If it starts sounding like "And so that's the way it happened, you idiot," stop. Same if the shame goes up or you start to feel unreal, and telling it colder or from farther away won't fix that. Then ask what the younger you in that story needs from you now.
t65t_sp5p2d6: This doesn't make the memory fiction or prove it right, and it doesn't let anyone off the hook. The trial ends; any repair that's owed is still owed, whoever owes it. If the line works, keep it to one line, and ask what the person in that story needs from you now.

t65t_sp7p2d2: Breathe however you normally breathe while you do it. And it isn't homework about anyone who hurt you. It's only a way to stop treating a feeling every human has as proof that you, in particular, are broken.
t65t_sp7p2e2: You don't need special breathing, and you go first in the wish, before anyone else who comes to mind. It's not a nudge to forgive whoever hurt you, or to picture their childhood, and it doesn't ask you to get in touch with anybody (that's its own decision, never one for while you're flooded). It just helps you put down the idea that a feeling this common proves something's wrong with you alone.

t65t_sp8p1e: Some people find that picturing their little one feels like making stuff up. If that's you, try digging out a real photo from back then. No inventing faces needed, since the little you is right there, in whatever outfit you got stuck with that year. Just look at it gently and notice what comes up, without deciding ahead of time what it has to prove.
t65t_sp8p2c: While you look, notice what your body does and what feelings or urges show up, and what that younger you seems to want you to get. Then sort it. Some of it you'll remember yourself, and some of it someone told you later ("You hated that coat"). Some you're guessing from the picture, and some might be an image or a dream, or you honestly don't know. Then ask what your little one needs from you now, and do a bit of it.
t65t_sp8p3c: And try not to ask it leading questions, like "What abuse must have happened?", "Who did this to me?" or "What memory is my body hiding?" Grilling one photo until a story shows up is a good way to get a story, but not necessarily a true one. Guided imagery and suggestive questions can create false memories. [In one study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/BF03196318), people shown a doctored photo of a childhood hot-air balloon ride they never took started remembering it, about half of them, at least partly.
t65t_sp8p3d: Some questions are better left alone: "What abuse must have happened?" "Who did this to me?" "What memory is my body hiding?" Those lead. So does staring at the same photo until a story finally turns up. Memory is suggestible like that. Guided imagery and suggestive questions can plant memories, and [in one experiment](https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/BF03196318), half the people shown a doctored childhood photo of a balloon ride came to remember the ride, at least partly. They'd never been in a balloon.
t65t_sp8p4c: Remember that somebody chose that moment and framed it. Whatever was happening outside the frame isn't in it, and neither is the reason you looked the way you did. A photo or a jolt in your body can say something real about how you feel today, the way a dream can, and still prove nothing about the story the photo seems to tell. So if it starts to look like something serious happened, don't confront or accuse anybody based on this alone. Write down exactly what came up and how, and talk it over with someone steady who won't lead you toward an answer.
t65t_sp8p5c: When you're done, put the photo away, every time. And the first time it starts pulling at you (searching it again, needing to be sure, or leaving you overwhelmed), stop using it for a while. Come back to the present and settle yourself there, with whatever usually helps you calm down.
t65t_sp8p5d: Put the photo back in its drawer when you're finished, good day or not. If it starts tugging at you, so you keep going back to search it or you need to know for sure, or you're getting overwhelmed, take a break from it right then. Settle yourself in the present first, the way you usually would.

At night, look back at the day the way you'd look over a friend's shoulder at theirs, kindly. Where did you notice the hook, and where did it run its whole routine anyway? What's the next small repair, or the next thing that would protect your little one?

Maybe you can think of a small repair, or something protective you could do next.

t65t_sp6p2h2: And what good did you get today? Count the small stuff, like a warm moment, or some nerve you didn't know you had. Noticing the hook counts too, and it counts if you're only seeing it now, in the review. Same if you broke the pattern somewhere. Then repair what you can, and that's the day. Same intention tomorrow. Bed.

Then pick the same intention for tomorrow and go to sleep, because the review's over.

## Borrow Hindsight

A question to borrow from your future self: "How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?" It can change how the whole thing looks. It can also just make you feel a bit more like that person, or less alone (sometimes all at once). Keep in mind it's only their best guess. No perfect Higher Self is handing down answers.

## One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night

In the morning, you could set one small intention, like "Today I'll notice one hook before I act on it." Any hook counts (it's harder than it sounds; hooks are sneaky). Maybe you can think of a small repair, or something protective you could do next.

## One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night

Mornings can start with one small intention. Nothing heroic: "Today I'll notice one hook before I act on it," whichever hook shows up first. At night, have a look back at the day, and try not to grade yourself while you do it. Where did you notice the hook? Where did it run the show anyway? And what's the next small repair, or the next thing that would protect your little one?
